QF.id: SIA Assessment Frameworks Techniques and Standards_27

question.text: A 95% confidence interval on an outcome proportion means:

answer.text: There is a 95% probability the true population proportion lies within the computed interval
If we repeated the sampling procedure many times, approximately 95% of the computed intervals would contain the true population proportion
95% of the sampled individuals reported the outcome
The outcome is statistically significant at the 5% level

explanation.text: The Logic: In classical (frequentist) statistics, the true population parameter is treated as a fixed unknown, not as a random variable. A 95% confidence interval is itself the random object - it depends on the particular sample drawn. The correct interpretation is therefore a statement about the long-run performance of the procedure: if the sampling and interval-construction procedure were repeated many times, approximately 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true population proportion. Any particular interval either does or does not contain the true value. The Trap: Option A ("a 95% probability the true value lies within the computed interval") is the most common intuitive misstatement - it is a Bayesian-flavoured reading and is not technically correct under the frequentist framework that underlies a confidence interval. Option C confuses a confidence interval with a sample statistic (the proportion of individuals reporting the outcome). Option D confuses a confidence interval with a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level. Note: The cited workbook pages (109, 131 of the Social Impact Assessors Certification Examination Workbook) refer to confidence in audit conclusions and to defining a confidence interval for sample-size calculation, but they do not state the frequentist interpretation of a 95% confidence interval as written in the correct option. The framing above reflects standard statistics/inferential-methodology practice that is treated as canonical across research-methods literature.
